page: Amazon Web Services r5n.16xlarge is a memory-optimized cloud server instance powered by the AWS Nitro System and built on 64-bit x86 architecture. The instance delivers 64 virtual CPU cores across 32 physical cores of an Intel Xeon 8259CL processor clocked at 3.1 GHz, supporting two threads per core. System memory is configured with 512.0 GB of DDR4 RAM running at 3 GHz, yielding an 8.0 GB allocation per core and a 1:8 vCPU-to-RAM ratio. Compute features include 35 MB of shared L3 cache, 1.0 MB L2 cache per core, and instruction set support for AVX-512 with VNNI, AES, and BMI2. No dedicated hardware GPUs or local storage devices are included on the host, making external block storage attachments necessary for persistent disk IO.

Network connectivity is a defining characteristic of the r5n family, supplying 75 Gbps of baseline network bandwidth. Benchmark evaluations reflect strong uncached memory bandwidth, reaching 217.82 GB/s on 256 MB read blocks and 96.29 GB/s on write blocks. PassMark database tests also score in the upper percentile at 21,748.64 operations, alongside PassMark extended vector instructions at 54,153.69. Conversely, single-thread performance benchmarks register in lower tiers, with a single-core Geekbench score of 1,121.0 and a stress-ng single-core rating of 1,286.19. Multi-core compute benchmarks reside in median ranges, recording a Geekbench multi-core mark of 11,686.0 and 50.71 million Redis SET operations per second.

From an infrastructure efficiency perspective, the r5n.16xlarge trades peak per-core processing efficiency for expansive memory capacity and high-throughput network transport. The lack of integrated NVMe drives directs input and output operations across the network fabric, where the 75 Gbps interface prevents pipeline bottlenecks. The server is configured for memory-intensive enterprise workloads, including large-scale in-memory databases like Redis or Memcached, distributed caching tiers, real-time analytics pipelines, and data warehouse ETL jobs requiring heavy network and RAM bandwidth.
